progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From B13: large samples give stronger inference, not certainty; a collaborative project pools data; heterozygote advantage. From B11: allele frequency = copies / all copies; association is not cause. From B9: autosomal dominant and recessive inheritance; carriers; each child of a heterozygous parent has a one in two chance of inheriting a given allele; a probability per child is not a guaranteed count. From B7: genes code for proteins; genotype and phenotype; environment can affect phenotype. From B4: DNA can be damaged and repaired (Year 11 and B4 level). Year 10 probability and square roots. Not assumed: risk pattern, the Hardy-Weinberg principle, carrier frequency estimates, the working-copy explanation.
progression.startsWith: The hook: A collaborative study from several countries followed nearly 10,000 women who carry a harmful version of a gene called BRCA1 or BRCA2. Among the BRCA1 carriers, about 72 in every 100 were estimated to get breast cancer by age 80.
progression.stopsAfter: reading a cohort estimate as a proportion of a group (about 72 in 100 BRCA1 carriers by age 80) and saying it cannot say which individuals; explaining why a variant raises risk without deciding the outcome (a working second copy must also be lost; other genes, environment and chance); saying that higher probability is not certainty and a negative result is not a guarantee; estimating a carrier frequency from the incidence of a recessive condition (q squared, q, p, 2pq) and explaining why carriers cannot be counted directly; stating the Hardy-Weinberg conditions, that deviation shows a force acting, and that predictions hold best in large populations over short times; explaining why a genetic result also gives information about relatives (one in two for each child, with the 2003 Icelandic ruling as a consequence); using strong, cautious wording; applying this to an unseen overclaim and an unseen carrier estimate.
progression.nextLesson: Module 6, how mutation and technology change these patterns (route entry bio-m6-genetic-change-route).

teaching.task: If a big study shows that carriers of a variant are at high risk, what can that predict for a group, and what can't it tell one person?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why a proportion cannot name individuals (it is measured across a group, 2); why one faulty copy does not decide the outcome (a working copy must also be lost, by chance, 3); why a negative result is no guarantee (most cases have other causes, 4); why carriers cannot be counted but can be estimated (they look healthy; affected babies reveal q squared; two ways to be a carrier, 5); why predictions fail in small populations (chance pushes frequencies either way, 6); why relatives share risk (one in two per child, 7). Visible case: one dot array, one chromosome pair and cell row, one stage column, one pedigree. Video advantage: dots fill and then lose their identity; one cell loses its working copy; the stage column builds; drift traces wander live. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items with every value and demand on screen. Reading load: scene 5 is the densest and builds one stage per cue with earlier results retained small.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Opens on the hook (hook (seventy-two in a hundred)), then works through a group proportion, not one person's future, why the gene doesn't decide on its own, probability isn't certainty, a population prediction that works, when population predictions hold and the remaining scenes in order, with each reasoning stage shown on its own cue; ends with the unseen attempt (10 second countdown), brief feedback, the decision rule or board, and the key notes.
teaching.openingDecision: A collaborative study from several countries followed nearly 10,000 women who carry a harmful version of a gene called BRCA1 or BRCA2. Among the BRCA1 carriers, about 72 in every 100 were estimated to get breast cancer by age 80. So does carrying that variant mean a woman will get breast cancer? And can population genetics predict anything with real accuracy?
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is a cohort finding (carriers develop heart disease twice as often) with an overclaiming report about one carrier: it tests what group data support, the rewrite, and the relative-risk trap. 10c is a Hardy-Weinberg carrier estimate from a new incidence (1 in 10,000) with a reliability demand for a small isolated village: it transfers scene 5's stages and scene 6's assumptions. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; each card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reason, short working, one crossed-out classic mistake. No mark-allocation talk.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (2017, BIO12-12, programme/syllabus/bio-2017-y12.json, B5-IQ5-03, p 50, inquiry question IQ5): "investigate the use of data analysis from a large-scale collaborative project to identify trends, patterns and relationships, for example: (ACSBL064, ACSBL073)", example "population genetics studies used to determine the inheritance of a disease or disorder" (B5-IQ5-05). Inquiry question: "Can population genetic patterns be predicted with any accuracy?" Route action B-collaborative-data (shared with B13). The two spaces before "for example" are in the official DOCX extraction.

design.visualSystem: Three boards. (1) The risk board (scenes 1 to 4): a coded 10 x 10 dot array (dots, never people icons), with filled and open dots computed from the cohort proportion; a coded chromosome pair for the working-copy explanation; a coded cell row for "a cell also loses that copy". (2) The calculation board (scenes 5, 6): the task line, a givens group, a stage column; a coded population bar for affected, carriers and non-carriers (computed); a coded allele-frequency trace for large and small populations (B11's seeded rng sampling, illustrative). (3) The family and wording board (scenes 7, 8): B9's pedigree with one-in-two tags; a coded Iceland outline chip; a two-column strong and weak wording card. Amber is the emphasis colour only.
design.transitionPlan: The risk board (a 10 by 10 dot array) opens the lesson and carries scenes 1 to 4; the Hardy-Weinberg and conditions board builds in scenes 5 and 6; the relatives and wording boards follow in scenes 7 and 8; each attempt card clears the board and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and builds the model answer one point at a time; the next chip slides in; scene crossfade with settle.

scenes.teachingReason: Hook (seventy-two in a hundred): A collaborative study from several countries followed nearly 10,000 women who carry a harmful version of a gene called BRCA1 or BRCA2.
scenes.narrationCue: BRCA1 or BRCA2 / about 72 in every 100 / will get breast cancer?
scenes.motionPurpose: B13's m5x-sample-tube-rack-v1.png sits small at the left; five coded site badges with country chips ("UK", "Netherlands", "France", "Australia", "North America"; tag "and other countries"; tag "BRCA cohort consortium") send streams into one bar with a counter to "nearly 10,000 carriers". On "BRCA1 or BRCA2" a coded chromosome bar appears with one locus marked (tag "BRCA1: a gene").
scenes.onScreenChange: the risk board. B13's m5x-sample-tube-rack-v1.png sits small at the left; five coded site badges with country chips ("UK", "Netherlands", "France", "Australia", "North America"; tag "and other countries"; tag "BRCA cohort consortium") send streams into one bar with a counter to "nearly 10,000 carriers". On "BRCA1 or BRCA2" a coded chromosome bar appears with one locus marked (tag "BRCA1: a gene"). On "about 72 in every 100" a large coded DotArray of 100 dots draws, and 72 fill one by one in seeded random order (tag "estimated, by age 80"; source tag "Kuchenbaecker et al. 2017"). On "will get breast cancer?" one open dot and one filled dot each get a "?". The heading writes on: "Risk is not destiny". Hold two seconds.

scenes.visualReference: on "100 dots" the array tidies into a 10 x 10 block; on "About 72" the filled dots count to 72 (computed) and on "about 28" the open dots count to 28.
scenes.teachingReason: A group proportion, not one person's future: Here's what that number really says.
scenes.narrationCue: 100 dots / About 72 / about 28 / measured across thousands / another large group / which dots are which / a probability, not a forecast
scenes.motionPurpose: On "measured across thousands" the array briefly shrinks into one tile of a huge mosaic of similar tiles (tag "thousands of carriers"; grey tag "B13: big data sharpen the trend"). On "another large group" a second 100-dot array draws beside it, filling to 71 (seeded; tag "a new group: close to the same proportion").
scenes.onScreenChange: on "100 dots" the array tidies into a 10 x 10 block; on "About 72" the filled dots count to 72 (computed) and on "about 28" the open dots count to 28. On "measured across thousands" the array briefly shrinks into one tile of a huge mosaic of similar tiles (tag "thousands of carriers"; grey tag "B13: big data sharpen the trend"). On "another large group" a second 100-dot array draws beside it, filling to 71 (seeded; tag "a new group: close to the same proportion"). The term "risk pattern" writes on with the gloss "how likely, across a group". On "which dots are which" every dot turns grey and a single dot is picked out with an amber ring and a "?" (tag "this person: filled or open? unknown"). On "a probability, not a forecast" the tag "about 72% chance by 80" writes beside the ringed dot. Hold one second.

scenes.teachingReason: Why the gene doesn't decide on its own: So why can't the gene decide on its own?
scenes.narrationCue: repair damaged DNA / one faulty copy / a cell also loses that working copy / chance damage, other genes and other factors / raises the risk
scenes.motionPurpose: On "repair damaged DNA" a short coded DNA strip with a nick is mended by a small repair-protein blob (tag "BRCA1 protein: DNA repair"). On "one faulty copy" a chromosome pair appears in B5b's plum and teal: the plum copy's BRCA1 locus is marked with a grey cross (tag "faulty copy, inherited"), the teal copy's locus glows (tag "working copy"); a grey tag under the pair: "inherited like a dominant trait; in a cell, bot
scenes.onScreenChange: WorkingCopy. On "repair damaged DNA" a short coded DNA strip with a nick is mended by a small repair-protein blob (tag "BRCA1 protein: DNA repair"). On "one faulty copy" a chromosome pair appears in B5b's plum and teal: the plum copy's BRCA1 locus is marked with a grey cross (tag "faulty copy, inherited"), the teal copy's locus glows (tag "working copy"); a grey tag under the pair: "inherited like a dominant trait; in a cell, both copies must fail". On "a cell also loses that working copy" a row of 20 coded cells appears, each carrying the pair; one cell's teal locus flickers out by chance (seeded) and that cell darkens (tag "both copies lost: this cell can become a cancer"). On "chance damage, other genes and other factors" three small tags write on around the row: "chance", "other genes", "other factors: hormones, age" (grey tag "B7: environment affects phenotype"). On "raises the risk" a single chip writes on: "variant: raises risk, doesn't fix the outcome". Hold one second.

scenes.visualReference: on "isn't a certain outcome" a chip "carrier, so she will get cancer" writes on and takes a grey scribble cross.
scenes.teachingReason: Probability isn't certainty: So a higher probability isn't a certain outcome.
scenes.narrationCue: isn't a certain outcome / Most women who get breast cancer / testing negative for a BRCA variant / not genetic destiny
scenes.motionPurpose: On "Most women who get breast cancer" a second coded DotArray of 100 dots draws, labelled "women with breast cancer", with about 2 dots amber-edged (tag "BRCA carriers: about 2 in 100"; grey source tag "population studies"). On "testing negative for a BRCA variant" the chip "no variant, so no cancer" writes on and takes a grey scribble cross.
scenes.onScreenChange: on "isn't a certain outcome" a chip "carrier, so she will get cancer" writes on and takes a grey scribble cross. On "Most women who get breast cancer" a second coded DotArray of 100 dots draws, labelled "women with breast cancer", with about 2 dots amber-edged (tag "BRCA carriers: about 2 in 100"; grey source tag "population studies"). On "testing negative for a BRCA variant" the chip "no variant, so no cancer" writes on and takes a grey scribble cross. On "not genetic destiny" the line writes on in hand type: "genetic risk is not genetic destiny". Hold one second.

scenes.teachingReason: A population prediction that works: Population predictions can be very accurate, though.
scenes.narrationCue: can't be counted by looking / one baby in 2,500 / times itself is one in 2,500 / Take the square root / the normal allele's is 0.98 / two ways to get that / two times 0.98 times 0.02
scenes.motionPurpose: The painted blood-spot card (m5x-newborn-blood-spot-card-v1.png, new) sits small at the upper left (tag "newborn screening"). The task writes on at the top: "How common are carriers?" On "can't be counted by looking" three coded genotype chips appear, "two normal", "carrier", "two CF alleles", the first two drawn identically healthy (tag "carriers look the same").
scenes.onScreenChange: the calculation board. The painted blood-spot card (m5x-newborn-blood-spot-card-v1.png, new) sits small at the upper left (tag "newborn screening"). The task writes on at the top: "How common are carriers?" On "can't be counted by looking" three coded genotype chips appear, "two normal", "carrier", "two CF alleles", the first two drawn identically healthy (tag "carriers look the same"). On "one baby in 2,500" the givens group writes on: "affected babies: 1 in 2,500 (two copies)" and "CF: recessive". Then one stage at a time in the stage column, each on its cue, earlier results retained small at the left: (1) on "times itself is one in 2,500": "q squared = 1/2,500 = 0.0004" with the glosses "q = CF allele frequency" and "from mother AND from father: q x q" (grey tag "B11: counting alleles"); (2) on "Take the square root": "q = 0.02"; (3) on "the normal allele's is 0.98": "p = 1 minus q = 0.98"; (4) on "two ways to get that" two small arrows show "CF from mother, normal from father" and "normal from mother, CF from father"; (5) on "two times 0.98 times 0.02": "carriers = 2pq = 2 x 0.98 x 0.02 = 0.039" and on "about one person in 25" "about 1 in 25" (all computed). On "Hardy-Weinberg principle" the name writes on above the stage column, with the gloss "allele frequencies predict genotype frequencies, if nothing disturbs them". On "rare disease, common carriers" a PopBar draws: a hair-thin "affected" slice, a visible "carriers" slice and a long "neither" bar (computed widths; tag "rare disease, common carriers"). Grey tag at the lower right: "example figures, similar to cystic fibrosis in some populations". Hold one second.

scenes.visualReference: the stage column dims; a checklist writes on, one line per cue: "large population", "random mating", "no selection", "no migration", "no new mutations" (tag "Hardy-Weinberg conditions").
scenes.teachingReason: When population predictions hold: But that estimate only holds if the population is large, mates at random, and isn't changed by selection, migration or new mutations.
scenes.narrationCue: that's useful too / DNA tests give the allele's frequency / more babies are affected than it predicts / a large population over a short time / In a small population
scenes.motionPurpose: On "that's useful too" the tag "a gap between prediction and data means something is acting" writes on. On "DNA tests give the allele's frequency" a small coded DNA-test chip writes "q from DNA tests" and a bar "predicted affected (from DNA tests: q x q)" draws; on "more babies are affected than it predicts" an "observed affected" bar grows past it, the gap ringed amber (illustrative), and a small two-symbol marriage
scenes.onScreenChange: the stage column dims; a checklist writes on, one line per cue: "large population", "random mating", "no selection", "no migration", "no new mutations" (tag "Hardy-Weinberg conditions"). On "that's useful too" the tag "a gap between prediction and data means something is acting" writes on. On "DNA tests give the allele's frequency" a small coded DNA-test chip writes "q from DNA tests" and a bar "predicted affected (from DNA tests: q x q)" draws; on "more babies are affected than it predicts" an "observed affected" bar grows past it, the gap ringed amber (illustrative), and a small two-symbol marriage line with a double bar (pedigree convention for related parents) appears (tag "relatives having children: not random mating"). On "a large population over a short time" DriftTraces draws: five allele-frequency traces for a population of 10,000 stay close to their start of 0.1 across 50 generations (seeded; tag "large: stays close"). On "In a small population" five traces for a population of 20, also starting at 0.1, wander up and down in steps of 1/40, some hitting zero (seeded; tag "illustrative starting frequency"; tag "small: chance pushes it either way"; grey tag "genetic drift: Module 6"). Hold one second.

scenes.teachingReason: Risk is shared with relatives: Genetic risk is also shared within families.
scenes.narrationCue: each of her children / brothers and sisters / one of her parents / never only about one person / Iceland's Supreme Court
scenes.motionPurpose: B9's Pedigree builds: I-1 open square, I-2 circle with a small amber dot (tag "carrier"); II-1 the woman (circle with amber dot, amber ring), II-2 brother, II-3 sister; III-1 and III-2 her children. On "each of her children" tags "1 in 2" pin under III-1 and III-2 (grey tag "B9: one in two per child").
scenes.onScreenChange: the family board. B9's Pedigree builds: I-1 open square, I-2 circle with a small amber dot (tag "carrier"); II-1 the woman (circle with amber dot, amber ring), II-2 brother, II-3 sister; III-1 and III-2 her children. On "each of her children" tags "1 in 2" pin under III-1 and III-2 (grey tag "B9: one in two per child"). On "brothers and sisters" tags "1 in 2" pin under II-2 and II-3; on "one of her parents" I-2's amber dot pulses (tag "a parent almost certainly carries it"; grey tag "unless it arose new in her"). Hold one second.

scenes.visualReference: the WordingCard writes on in two columns, one phrase per cue.
scenes.teachingReason: Strong and weak wording: So in an exam, match your claim to your evidence.
scenes.narrationCue: don't write that carriers will get the disease / more likely / precise and cautious
scenes.motionPurpose: Left "strong": "suggests a trend", "indicates increased risk", "more likely in this population". Right "weak": "proves every individual will", "guarantees", "removes all uncertainty", each struck through in grey as it lands.

scenes.visualReference: three handwritten lines write on with small icons: "population evidence, population conclusions" (the 100-dot array), "genetic risk is not genetic destiny" (the single ringed dot), "rare disease, common carriers" (the PopBar).
